paragraphs.heading: What a mass extinction is
paragraphs.text: An extinction event, also called a mass extinction, is a fast and widespread drop in the variety of life on Earth. Scientists recognise one by a sharp fall in how many kinds of many-celled organisms there are and how plentiful they are. It happens when species die out faster than the normal background rate, and faster than new species form.

paragraphs.heading: How many there have been
paragraphs.text: Over the past 540 million years, counts of major mass extinctions run from as few as five to more than twenty. The counts differ because experts disagree about what makes an event major, and about which data best measure past diversity. Careful statistical tests have shown that animal life in the present eon, the Phanerozoic, has been through at least five major mass extinctions and many smaller ones. These Big Five look less like a separate group and more like the largest points on a fairly smooth range of events.

paragraphs.heading: The Late Ordovician
paragraphs.text: The Late Ordovician mass extinction probably came in two pulses. The first matched a cooling and a large glaciation in the south, and the second came with the thaw. Together they killed 27% of families, 57% of genera and 85% of species, so many scientists rank it second of the five by share of genera lost. Its cause is still argued over. Studies in 2020 pointed to warming tied to volcanoes and to anoxia, meaning seawater stripped of oxygen, while many earlier studies blamed cooling.

paragraphs.heading: The Late Devonian
paragraphs.text: The Late Devonian lost much of its diversity in two big events. The larger, the Kellwasser Event about 372 million years ago, wiped out coral reefs and many tropical sea-floor animals, such as jawless fish, brachiopods and trilobites. Many scientists think rivers carried nutrients from land into the sea, feeding huge blooms of algae, and as the algae died and rotted they used up the oxygen in the water. The second, the Hangenberg Event about 359 million years ago, ended the Devonian, wiped out the armoured placoderm fish and almost finished off the ammonoids.

paragraphs.heading: The Great Dying
paragraphs.text: The largest extinction of the Phanerozoic was the End Permian extinction, known as the Great Dying, where the Permian gives way to the Triassic. In the seas, 53% of families, 84% of genera and about 81% of species died. On land an estimated 70% of species of backboned animals were lost. It is also the largest known extinction event for insects, and it ended the trilobites, a very successful group of sea arthropods, along with leading groups of corals.

paragraphs.heading: What came after
paragraphs.text: The Great Dying changed the course of evolution. On land it cut short many lines of synapsids, the relatives of mammals. Backboned animals took 30 million years to recover, but the empty niches gave archosaurs, relatives of dinosaurs and crocodiles, room to spread into many forms. In the seas, the share of animals fixed in one place fell from 67% to 50%. Yet the damage on land may have been milder than once thought: a 2025 study in China found a thriving ecosystem only 75,000 years later.
